newsitem.title: USA: For-profit, nonprofit hospitals similar - study.
newsitem.headline: For-profit, nonprofit hospitals similar - study.

text.p: Investor-owned for-profit hospitals may not be all that different from the more familiar nonprofit institutions, according to a new study released Wednesday.
The $400,000 study was financed by the Federation of American Health Systems, a for-profit hospital group, but was carried out by consultants at the independent Project Hope.
The study consisted of review of national data, as well as 10 case studies in hospitals in different settings around the country.
Between 1987-1997, 87 hospitals converted from nonprofit to for-profit status. Numerous other hospitals merged, and some were closed during that decade.

Conversions have been controversial for numerous reasons, including concern about monopolies and fears that charity care would be cut and overall patient care take second place to profits. Communities may lack a voice in the conversions, and the study found that many of the deals were put together with little public input or regulatory oversight.

Defenders say that the for-profit hospitals tend to be more efficient, pay taxes to the community and bring in capital for modernization and improvement of health facilities, and may save ailing hospitals from closing.

The authors said much more research is needed in this rapidly changing field, particularly to assess the quality of health care, but their study did not find any trends toward serious problems when hospitals become investor-owned.

"In and of itself, conversion doesn't cause problems," said Marc Berk, the project director. Researcher Tami Mark said that hospitals that allow themselves to be acquired by for-profit companies tend to be in poor financial shape and the change in status may be a response to the "cost-cutting pressures from managed care companies, third party payors and public sector payors," such as Medicare.

After conversion, the hospitals tended to be in better financial shape. It was difficult to precisely measure how much charity care and community services the hospitals were providing, although there was some evidence that at least in the short-term they were providing similar levels.

But there were also problems, as Federation president Tom Scully acknowledged in a briefing for reporters. For instance, at Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp's Cedars Medical Center in Miami, employee morale has worsened since the for-profit takeover, he said..
"The results are a very mixed bag," said Scully. "But the differences between investor-owned and community-owned (hospitals) are vastly overblown."
